title: OpenAI Advances Chip Design with AI Models, Achieving 14% PPA Improvement for AMD GPU
summary: OpenAI achieves 14% PPA improvement for AMD GPU using AI chip design models
detailed: OpenAI released a technical report detailing the use of AI models to optimize chip design for its proprietary Jalapeño inference chip and AMD hardware.
The AI models achieved up to a 14% improvement in performance, power, and area (PPA) on AMD's flagship GPU IP and reduced standard cell area in Jalapeño compute units by 10% to 15%.
Key players involved include OpenAI and AMD, with testing also utilizing open-source RISC-V processors like PicoRV32 and Ibex.
This matters because the technology successfully compressed about a year of hardware design optimization into less than five months, demonstrating AI's viability in silicon engineering.
sentences: On November 18 local time, OpenAI released its latest technical report, "Advancing Chip Design with OpenAI Models," disclosing recent progress in using AI models to assist in chip design.

According to reports, OpenAI has applied the relevant technology to its proprietary inference chip, Jalapeño, and to the design optimization of AMD’s next-generation GPUs and CPUs, while also using open-source RISC-V processors to test and evaluate chip design capabilities across different generations of models.
OpenAI stated that engineers began using GPT-4o to assist in designing Jalapeño as early as early 2025.
Even at that time, the model was already capable of proposing substantial improvements in chip performance, power, and area (PPA).
In Jalapeño’s vector computation unit, AI models reduce hardware resource usage by optimizing floating-point adders, multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and special function units.
In the matrix computation unit, the AI model successfully improved floating-point operations and low-precision dot product circuits.

One redesigned multiplier reduced the synthesized standard cell area by approximately 15% while reducing operational latency from two clock cycles to one; another adder design also reduced the standard cell area by approximately 15% while maintaining a two-clock-cycle latency.
OpenAI estimates that the model's proposed modifications reduced the standard cell area of the Jalapeño vector compute unit by approximately 13% and the matrix compute unit by approximately 10%.
These optimizations have been validated on actual silicon.
In collaboration with AMD, OpenAI models also contributed to optimizing GPU and CPU chip designs.
OpenAI reported that, on AMD’s flagship GPU IP, the models achieved up to a 14% improvement in PPA compared to a highly optimized baseline design.
The models further optimized circuit structures by rewriting the SystemVerilog RTL code that describes chip circuits.
OpenAI stated that this equates to compressing approximately one year of design optimization progress into less than five months.
AMD has incorporated some of the optimizations into chip designs recently submitted for manufacturing, while other modifications have been added to production design files for use in future products.
Additionally, AMD has validated that the model has delivered single-digit percentage PPA improvements in key modules of its next-generation flagship CPU.

To evaluate the ability of different generations of AI models to independently complete chip design tasks, OpenAI selected two open-source 32-bit RISC-V processor cores for testing: PicoRV32, designed for FPGAs, and Ibex, the embedded processor used in the OpenTitan security chip.
During testing, OpenAI provided the model with raw hardware description code and asked it to improve processor throughput, while verifying design correctness through simulation.

For designs that passed the verification, researchers calculated instructions per second by combining the number of instructions per clock cycle under hidden test loads with the maximum clock frequency estimated by Yosys.
Designs that failed the correctness check or exceeded 16 times the area of the original design were scored as zero.
Test results show that, under a budget of approximately 112,000 tokens per run, GPT-6.2 Astra achieved the highest average scores on both the PicoRV32 and Ibex processors.
When optimizing based on the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT-6.2 Astra scored approximately twice as high as GPT-6 Astra under a similar budget.

OpenAI also conducted another test: instead of asking the model to optimize existing processors, it provided written specifications and code templates, instructing the model to design a RISC-V processor core from scratch, independently determining data flow and pipeline stage divisions.
In this task, all five models tested scored higher than the performance achieved when optimizing the existing design, under a runtime budget of approximately 112,000 tokens.
The evaluation covered two design tasks, two processor cores, and varying token budgets, comprising a total of 9,881 scoring runs.

However, OpenAI also noted that when redesigning the processor from specifications, the model may omit features such as performance counters and additional instructions present in the original chip, as these features offer limited benefit toward achieving throughput targets in testing, which may partially explain the improved scores.

If the model were required to retain these features, further constrain the circuit area, and verify timing after physical synthesis, the test results would more closely resemble actual mass-production chip design scenarios.

In terms of future plans, OpenAI announced a partnership with Synopsys, a provider of electronic design automation (EDA) software, to train a new model called GPT-Synopsys capable of using Synopsys’ EDA tools to perform chip design and verification tasks like a professional chip designer.

OpenAI stated that this research demonstrates AI models can not only explore new processor architectures but also propose further optimizations based on complex, mass-produced designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next-generation flagship GPUs and CPUs.
